papers.title: A kinetic-aware approach to infer metabolic variations and flux using transcriptomics and metabolomics data
papers.summary: This paper presents a computational method that integrates transcriptomics and metabolomics data while accounting for enzyme kinetics to better estimate metabolic flux and variations in biological systems. Traditional approaches often ignore kinetic constraints, leading to inaccurate flux predictions; this method aims to improve biological realism by incorporating kinetic principles. The approach could be applied broadly across tissue types and conditions to model how gene expression changes translate into actual metabolic activity.
papers.why: This method could help link spatial transcriptomics and spatial metabolomics data in neurons and interneurons to infer functional metabolic flux changes relevant to mitophagy and autophagy processes.

papers.title: Icariin enhances PINK1-associated mitophagy to attenuate NLRP3/GSDMD-related microglial pyroptosis and cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how the natural compound Icariin affects brain cells in a model of Alzheimer's disease. The researchers found that Icariin boosts PINK1-mediated mitophagy, a process that clears damaged mitochondria, in microglia (the brain's immune cells). This enhanced mitophagy reduces harmful inflammatory cell death (pyroptosis) driven by the NLRP3/GSDMD pathway, and improves cognitive function in affected models.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it directly examines PINK1-mediated mitophagy in brain cells within a neurodegenerative disease context, connecting mitochondrial quality control to neuroinflammation and cognitive outcomes, which parallels the project's focus on mitophagy mechanisms in neurons.

papers.title: Spatial cell-cell communication inference based on cell-spot-ligand-receptor heterogeneous graphs.
papers.summary: This paper presents a computational method that models spatial transcriptomics data as a heterogeneous graph linking cells, spatial spots, ligands, and receptors to infer cell-cell communication. By integrating these different node types into one graph structure, the approach aims to more accurately capture signaling interactions that depend on spatial proximity. The method likely outputs predicted ligand-receptor interactions between specific cell types localized within the tissue architecture.
papers.why: This tool could help map how interneurons communicate with surrounding glial and neuronal populations in spatially resolved brain tissue, potentially revealing signaling pathways relevant to perineuronal net remodeling and autophagy-related neuron-glia crosstalk.

papers.title: Enabling subcellular DESI-MSI for broad adoption: Acquisition, analysis, and application
papers.summary: This paper describes methods to make subcellular-resolution desorption electrospray ionization mass spectrometry imaging (DESI-MSI) more accessible to researchers. It covers improvements in data acquisition, computational analysis pipelines, and example applications of the technique. The goal is to lower technical barriers so more labs can use high-resolution spatial metabolomics at the subcellular level.
papers.why: Subcellular spatial metabolomics tools like this could allow direct mapping of mitochondrial and autophagy-related metabolites within neurons and perineuronal net microenvironments, complementing spatial transcriptomics data in your project.

papers.title: Targeting RUNX3 alleviates abdominal aortic aneurysm by ameliorating oxidative stress via mitophagy.
papers.summary: This paper studies abdominal aortic aneurysm, a vascular disease, and finds that a protein called RUNX3 contributes to the problem by increasing oxidative stress. The researchers show that blocking RUNX3 reduces aneurysm severity by boosting mitophagy, the process that clears out damaged mitochondria. This suggests RUNX3 could be a therapeutic target for treating this cardiovascular condition.
papers.why: Although focused on vascular disease rather than neurons, this paper's mechanistic insights into RUNX3-mediated mitophagy regulation and oxidative stress control could offer transferable concepts relevant to mitophagy pathways being studied in neuronal contexts.

papers.title: Protein Phosphatase Magnesium-Dependent 1H Exacerbates Intestinal Ischemia/Reperfusion Injury by Promoting FUN14 Domain-Containing 1-Dependent Mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study investigates how a protein called PPM1H affects intestinal damage caused by restricted blood flow followed by its return (ischemia/reperfusion injury). The researchers found that PPM1H worsens tissue damage by boosting a specific type of mitophagy, a process where damaged mitochondria are selectively cleared from cells, through activation of the FUNDC1 pathway. The findings suggest that blocking PPM1H or FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy could be a potential therapeutic strategy to reduce gut injury in these conditions.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on gut tissue rather than brain or neurons, the FUNDC1 mitophagy pathway it examines is directly relevant to understanding mitophagy regulatory mechanisms that could inform studies of neuronal mitochondrial quality control.

papers.title: hTERT associates with Rab7A to enhance autophagy and rescue oxLDL induced endothelial dysfunction
papers.summary: This paper studies hTERT, the catalytic subunit of telomerase, and shows it binds to Rab7A, a protein involved in late endosome/lysosome trafficking. This interaction enhances autophagy in endothelial cells. The enhanced autophagy helps protect endothelial cells from dysfunction caused by oxidized LDL, a key factor in atherosclerosis.
papers.why: This paper is about vascular endothelial cells and cardiovascular disease, which is only tangentially related to autophagy mechanisms in neurons and brain tissue relevant to this PhD project.
